title: Hot Flashes After Drinking: Causes, Menopause, and When to Worry
excerpt: Why alcohol makes you feel hot: blood-vessel widening, acetaldehyde, menopause hot flashes, night-time rebound, medication reactions, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why you get hot flashes after drinking alcohol: flushing, acetaldehyde, menopause triggers, night sweats, medication reactions, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** feeling a sudden wave of heat after drinking is common, and for most people it's harmless. Alcohol widens the small blood vessels near your skin, which pushes warm blood to the surface and makes you feel hot and flushed even as your core temperature actually drifts down. On top of that, a by-product of alcohol called acetaldehyde can trigger flushing, especially in people whose bodies clear it slowly. For women in perimenopause or menopause, alcohol is also a well-known trigger for hot flashes. A few less common causes are worth knowing about, including certain medications that react with alcohol and, rarely, medical conditions where flushing is the first clue.

**The quick rules:** If you get hot within minutes of a drink, that's usually blood-vessel widening or an acetaldehyde flush. If it hits in the night or the next morning, it's more often your body rebounding as the alcohol wears off. If you're in menopause and notice more hot flashes on nights you drink, alcohol is a reasonable suspect, and cutting back for two weeks is the simplest test. If the heat comes with a racing heart, throbbing headache, nausea, and vomiting after you started a new medicine, stop drinking and call a pharmacist or doctor.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US)** if hot flushing after a drink comes with trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, hives spreading across your body, chest pain, fainting, or confusion. Those can be signs of a serious allergic reaction or a heart problem. **Book a regular appointment** if you flush or get hot flashes after even small amounts of alcohol and you didn't used to, if the flushing comes with diarrhea, wheezing, or weight loss you can't explain, if you get drenching sweats on nights you didn't drink, or if you're having a strong reaction after starting a new medication. **If you drink heavily most days** and get sweats, shakes, a racing heart, or anxiety when you stop or cut back, that can be alcohol withdrawal. It can become dangerous, so talk to a doctor before stopping on your own.

## Why Alcohol Makes You Feel Hot

There are three overlapping reasons you can feel a rush of heat after drinking. Most people experience some mix of all three.

### 1. Alcohol opens up your blood vessels

Alcohol is a vasodilator, which means it relaxes and widens blood vessels. The effect is most noticeable in the small vessels near the surface of your skin, especially on your face, neck, and chest. More warm blood flows to the skin, nerve endings there sense the warmth, and your brain reads it as "I'm hot."

This is the same reason people once thought a shot of brandy would warm you up in the cold. It feels warming, but it's misleading. By sending blood to the skin, alcohol lets your body lose heat faster. So you can feel hot and flushed while your core temperature is actually dropping a little. That mismatch is part of why some people feel hot one minute and shivery the next.

### 2. Acetaldehyde, the by-product that causes flushing

Your liver breaks alcohol down in two steps. First, an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase turns alcohol into **acetaldehyde**. Then a second enzyme, **aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2)**, turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate.

Acetaldehyde is toxic, and it's a strong trigger for flushing. It prompts the release of histamine and other chemicals that widen blood vessels. When acetaldehyde builds up, the result is a warm, red face, sometimes with a fast heartbeat, a pounding headache, and nausea.

How much acetaldehyde builds up depends partly on your genes. Many people of East Asian descent carry a variant of the ALDH2 gene that makes the enzyme work much more slowly. For them, even one drink can cause an intense flush, often called "Asian flush" or "Asian glow." Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) covers the genetics in depth. The variant isn't the only reason acetaldehyde can pile up, though. Drinking quickly, drinking on an empty stomach, and certain medications can all push levels higher in anyone.

### 3. Your body reacts to the drink itself

Some of the heat has nothing to do with alcohol. Wine and beer contain histamine and other compounds that can widen blood vessels on their own. Red wine tends to have more histamine than white wine, and some people find it's the drink most likely to make them flush. Sugary mixers, spicy food at the bar, a warm crowded room, and dancing all add to the load. If you only feel hot with one type of drink, the drink itself may be the problem rather than alcohol in general. Our article on [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking) goes deeper into the visible flush.

## Hot Flashes After Drinking vs. a Normal Flush

People use "hot flash" loosely, and it helps to separate what's going on.

| What you notice | When it happens | Most likely cause |
|---|---|---|
| Warm, red face and neck within minutes | While drinking | Blood-vessel widening, acetaldehyde |
| Intense red flush plus fast heartbeat after one drink | While drinking | Slow ALDH2 enzyme (alcohol flush reaction) |
| Sudden waves of heat spreading over the chest and face, sometimes with sweating | Evening or night, more often in midlife women | Menopause hot flash triggered by alcohol |
| Waking up hot and sweaty at 3 or 4 a.m. | During sleep | Rebound as alcohol wears off |
| Clammy, hot-and-cold feeling the next day | Morning after | Hangover, dehydration, stress hormones |
| Flushing, pounding headache, vomiting after a new medicine | While drinking | Drug reaction with alcohol |

A classic menopause hot flash tends to start suddenly, spread upward over the chest, neck, and face, last a few minutes, and sometimes end with sweating and a chill. An alcohol flush is usually more of a steady warmth and redness that lasts as long as you keep drinking. You can have both at the same time.

## Hot Flashes After Drinking During Menopause

If you're in perimenopause (the years leading up to your last period) or menopause and you've noticed more hot flashes on nights you drink, you're not imagining it. Alcohol is one of the triggers that menopause guidance most often tells women to watch, alongside spicy food, caffeine, hot drinks, warm rooms, and stress. The North American Menopause Society (now called The Menopause Society) and the UK's NHS both list alcohol among common hot flash triggers.

### Why menopause makes you more sensitive

During menopause, falling and fluctuating estrogen levels affect the part of the brain that controls body temperature, called the hypothalamus. Normally, your body tolerates small changes in temperature without reacting. In menopause, that comfortable range narrows. A tiny rise in temperature that you wouldn't have noticed before is enough to set off a full cooling response: blood vessels in the skin open wide, your heart speeds up, and you sweat to shed heat. That's a hot flash.

Alcohol does exactly the kind of thing that can tip this narrow system over. It widens skin blood vessels and nudges skin temperature up. In a body with a hair-trigger thermostat, that can be enough to start a hot flash.

### What the research says

The research here is honestly mixed, and it's worth knowing that. Many women clearly report that alcohol sets off their hot flashes, and that's why it's on the trigger lists. But large population studies that looked at drinking habits and hot flashes overall have not all found the same thing. Some found more hot flashes in women who drank, some found no link, and a few even found fewer hot flashes among light drinkers. One possible explanation is that these studies measure average drinking habits across thousands of women, while triggers are personal. Alcohol can be a clear trigger for one woman and make no difference to another.

The practical takeaway: you don't need a study to tell you what happens in your own body. If you suspect alcohol, test it.

### A simple way to test it

1. **Keep a short log for two weeks.** Note what you drank, when, and how many hot flashes you had that evening and night. A notes app on your phone is fine.
2. **Then take two weeks off alcohol**, or switch to non-alcoholic drinks, and keep logging.
3. **Compare.** If the hot flashes drop noticeably, alcohol is one of your triggers. If they don't change, alcohol probably isn't the main driver, and you can look at other triggers.

If you find alcohol is a trigger but you don't want to give it up, many women find that limiting it to one drink, having it earlier in the evening, switching from red wine to something else, and keeping the bedroom cool helps.

### Alcohol, sleep, and night sweats in menopause

Alcohol and menopause can team up to wreck sleep. Menopause already causes night sweats, and alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night as it wears off. The result is waking at 3 a.m. hot, sweaty, and wide awake. If that's your pattern, see our guides on [night sweats after drinking](/never-hungover/night-sweats-after-drinking) and [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).

### Talk to your doctor if hot flashes are hard to live with

Hot flashes that disrupt your sleep, work, or mood are worth raising with a doctor. There are effective treatments, including hormone therapy and several non-hormone options. A doctor can help you weigh them against your own health history. If you already take a menopause medicine, ask whether alcohol affects it.

## Hot Flashes at Night After Drinking

Waking up hot in the middle of the night after a few drinks is one of the most common versions of this. The usual cause is **rebound**.

While alcohol is in your system, it has a sedating, calming effect on the brain. As your liver clears it, usually a few hours after your last drink, the brain swings the other way. Stress hormones rise, your heart rate goes up, your body temperature regulation gets a little erratic, and sleep becomes lighter. Many people wake up hot, sweaty, with a fast heartbeat, and then struggle to get back to sleep.

A few other things add to night-time heat:

- **Dehydration.** Alcohol makes you pass more urine, and dehydration makes it harder for your body to control temperature.
- **Late, heavy, or spicy food.** Digestion produces heat, and spicy food can trigger flushing on its own.
- **A warm room and heavy bedding.** After drinking, you're less able to regulate heat, so a warm bedroom matters more.
- **Low blood sugar.** Heavy drinking can lower blood sugar overnight, which can cause sweating and a shaky, hot feeling, especially if you skipped dinner.

If your heart is pounding when you wake up hot, our guide on [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains what's normal and what isn't.

## Hot Flashes the Next Day (Hangover Hot Flashes)

Feeling hot and cold the morning after is a hallmark of a hangover. Your body is still dealing with the after-effects: dehydration, poor sleep, some inflammation, and stress hormones that are elevated from the overnight rebound. Small things, like a hot shower, a coffee, or walking up stairs, can set off a wave of heat and sweat.

What usually helps:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Water is fine. An electrolyte drink helps if you were sick or sweated a lot.
- **Eat something.** It steadies blood sugar and settles the stress response.
- **Stay cool.** A lukewarm shower, light clothes, and a fan are better than piling on layers.
- **Skip the hair of the dog.** Another drink just delays the rebound.
- **Go easy on caffeine.** A normal cup is fine, but a lot of caffeine can make the jittery, sweaty feeling worse.

Hangover heat should fade over the day. If you're still getting hot flashes and sweats a day or two later, that's not a typical hangover and is worth a call to your doctor, particularly if you drink heavily most days (see the withdrawal note below).

## Hot Flashes After Drinking in Men

Hot flashes aren't only a women's issue. Men get the same alcohol flush from blood-vessel widening and acetaldehyde. But if a man is getting true hot flashes, the sudden spreading waves of heat with sweating, it's worth thinking about hormones.

The main causes of hot flashes in men are:

- **Low testosterone.** Testosterone levels that drop sharply can cause hot flashes, much as falling estrogen does in women.
- **Prostate cancer treatment.** Androgen deprivation therapy, which lowers testosterone on purpose, very commonly causes hot flashes. Alcohol can be a trigger, just as it is in menopause.
- **Certain medications and conditions**, including some antidepressants and, less often, thyroid problems.

Heavy drinking over the long term can also lower testosterone. If you're a man getting regular hot flashes, with or without alcohol, mention it to your doctor. It's an easy problem to check with a blood test.

## Medications That Cause Flushing With Alcohol

Some medicines change how your body handles alcohol and can cause a strong flushing reaction, sometimes called a "disulfiram-like" reaction. Disulfiram is a drug prescribed to make drinking unpleasant; it blocks the ALDH2 enzyme so acetaldehyde builds up. A few other drugs can cause a milder version of the same thing.

| Medication | What can happen with alcohol |
|---|---|
| **Metronidazole (Flagyl)** and **tinidazole** | Labels warn against alcohol during treatment and for a few days after because of possible flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache, and fast heartbeat |
| **Some older diabetes drugs**, such as chlorpropamide | Facial flushing with alcohol has been well described |
| **Topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus** (eczema creams) | Face flushing with alcohol is a listed side effect for some users |
| **Some antifungals and antibiotics** | Check your label; a few carry alcohol warnings |
| **Niacin (vitamin B3)** | Causes flushing on its own, and alcohol can make it worse |
| **Nitrates and some blood pressure medicines** | Both widen blood vessels, so the combination can cause flushing, dizziness, and low blood pressure |

This isn't a complete list. If you get hot, flushed, nauseated, or your heart pounds after drinking while taking a new medicine, stop drinking and ask a pharmacist or doctor. They can check your full medication list in a few minutes. For a broader look, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Can Antihistamines or Pepcid Stop the Flush?

Some people take an antihistamine before drinking to cut down on flushing, often a combination of an H1 blocker (like Zyrtec or Allegra) and an H2 blocker (like Pepcid). It can make the redness less visible because histamine is part of the flushing process.

The problem is that it hides the symptom without fixing the cause. If you flush because acetaldehyde is building up, the acetaldehyde is still there. Acetaldehyde is a known carcinogen, and research has linked the slow ALDH2 variant combined with regular drinking to a higher risk of esophageal cancer. Masking the flush can lead people to drink more than their body handles well. Our article on [Pepcid for Asian flush](/never-hungover/pepcid-for-asian-flush) explains the trade-offs in more detail, and [antihistamines and alcohol](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) covers the drowsiness risk of combining them.

## Less Common Causes Worth Knowing About

In a small number of people, flushing or hot flashes after alcohol are a clue to something else going on. These are rare, so don't jump to them first, but they're worth knowing because they're easy to miss.

- **Rosacea.** Alcohol is a common trigger for rosacea flares, which cause redness and a hot, burning feeling in the face. If your face stays red between drinks, a dermatologist can help.
- **Alcohol intolerance or sensitivity to ingredients.** Some people react to sulfites, histamine, grains, or other components of a particular drink. Our guide on [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) covers one piece of this.
- **Thyroid problems.** An overactive thyroid can make you heat-intolerant and sweaty in general, and alcohol can make that more noticeable.
- **Carcinoid syndrome and mastocytosis.** These are rare conditions where the body releases flushing chemicals. Alcohol is a known trigger in both. Typical extra clues are flushing that comes with diarrhea, wheezing, or a racing heart, sometimes with weight loss.
- **Some blood cancers.** Rarely, pain or flushing after drinking alcohol has been reported as an early sign of Hodgkin lymphoma, especially pain in lymph nodes after drinking. It's uncommon, but if you notice pain in swollen glands after a drink, see a doctor.

The common thread: a new reaction you didn't used to have, or flushing that comes with other symptoms, deserves a check-up.

## A Note on Sweats, Shakes, and Withdrawal

Most people who search for this are social drinkers who had a few drinks and felt hot. That's normal and nothing to worry about. But it's worth saying clearly: if you drink heavily on most days and get hot flashes, sweating, shaking, a racing heart, anxiety, or trouble sleeping when you cut back or stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal. Withdrawal can become dangerous, including seizures in severe cases. Don't push through it alone. Talk to a doctor before stopping, and go to an emergency room if you have confusion, hallucinations, a seizure, or a very fast heartbeat.

## How to Reduce Hot Flashes and Flushing When You Drink

There's no trick that makes alcohol stop widening blood vessels. But you can reduce how often and how badly the heat hits.

1. **Drink less, and drink slower.** Acetaldehyde builds up when alcohol arrives faster than your liver can process it. Spacing drinks out, about one per hour or less, gives your liver time to keep up.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption, which slows the rise in acetaldehyde.
3. **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace and helps with dehydration.
4. **Notice your drink.** If red wine is the problem, try white wine or a clear spirit with a low-sugar mixer and see if it's different.
5. **Keep cool.** Lighter clothes, a cool room, and fresh air help, especially if you're in menopause.
6. **Drink earlier, not right before bed.** Giving alcohol a few hours to clear before sleep can reduce the 3 a.m. rebound.
7. **Skip the spicy food on drinking nights** if you notice it makes the heat worse.
8. **Check your medications** for alcohol warnings.

For more habits with good evidence behind them, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take when they drink. Lab and animal research suggests it may help the liver process alcohol and acetaldehyde, and it has been studied for its effects on the brain's response to alcohol. The human evidence is limited, so treat it as something that may help some people rather than a sure thing.

To be clear about what it won't do: there is no good evidence that DHM stops hot flashes, prevents a menopause hot flash, or switches off the genetic alcohol flush. It also doesn't make drinking safer for people with the slow ALDH2 variant. Drinking less is still the most reliable fix.

If you want to try it as part of a more moderate approach to drinking, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you're in menopause or on any medication, check with your doctor first; our article on [DHM and women's hormonal considerations](/never-hungover/dhm-women-hormonal-considerations-safety-2025) covers what is and isn't known.

## The Bottom Line

- Feeling hot after drinking is usually harmless. Alcohol widens skin blood vessels, and acetaldehyde adds to the flush.
- Hot flashes at night or the next morning are usually a rebound as the alcohol wears off, made worse by dehydration and poor sleep.
- In menopause, alcohol is a common hot flash trigger. The research is mixed overall, so test it on yourself with a two-week break.
- In men, true hot flashes can point to low testosterone or hormone treatment and are worth raising with a doctor.
- A strong flush with a pounding heart, headache, and vomiting after starting a new medicine needs a call to a pharmacist or doctor.
- Get emergency care for trouble breathing, swelling, chest pain, or fainting. If you drink heavily most days and get sweats and shakes when you stop, talk to a doctor before quitting.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get hot flashes after drinking alcohol?**

Alcohol widens the small blood vessels near your skin, sending warm blood to the surface so you feel hot and look flushed. A by-product of alcohol called acetaldehyde adds to the flush, especially in people whose bodies clear it slowly. Histamine in wine and beer, warm rooms, and spicy food can add to it. In menopause, alcohol can set off true hot flashes because the body's temperature control is more sensitive.

**Can alcohol trigger hot flashes during menopause?**

Yes, for many women. Menopause guidance from groups like The Menopause Society and the NHS lists alcohol as a common hot flash trigger. Large studies have had mixed results, which suggests alcohol is a strong trigger for some women and not for others. The easiest way to find out is to log your hot flashes for two weeks with your usual drinking and two weeks without alcohol, then compare.

**Why do I wake up hot at night after drinking?**

It's usually rebound. Alcohol has a calming effect while it's in your system, and as your liver clears it a few hours later, stress hormones rise, your heart speeds up, and your sleep gets lighter. That often wakes people up hot and sweaty around 3 or 4 a.m. Dehydration, a warm room, and drinking close to bedtime make it worse.

**Do men get hot flashes from alcohol?**

Men get the same alcohol flush from widened blood vessels and acetaldehyde. True hot flashes in men, with sudden waves of heat and sweating, are more often linked to low testosterone or prostate cancer treatment that lowers testosterone, and alcohol can trigger them in those cases. A man with regular hot flashes should mention it to a doctor, who can check hormone levels with a blood test.

**Is it bad if my face gets hot and red when I drink?**

Usually it's harmless, but it's worth paying attention to. A strong flush after one or two drinks often means acetaldehyde is building up, which is common in people with a slow version of the ALDH2 enzyme. Regular drinking with that variant has been linked to a higher risk of esophageal cancer, so a strong flush is a good reason to drink less rather than to hide it with antihistamines.

**Can medications cause hot flashes when you drink?**

Yes. Some medicines, including metronidazole (Flagyl), tinidazole, some older diabetes drugs, and topical eczema creams like tacrolimus, can cause flushing, nausea, headache, or a fast heartbeat with alcohol. Niacin and some blood pressure medicines can also make flushing worse. If you react after starting a new medicine, stop drinking and ask a pharmacist or doctor.

**When should I see a doctor about hot flashes after drinking?**

Get emergency help for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, widespread hives, chest pain, fainting, or confusion. Book an appointment if you suddenly react to small amounts of alcohol when you didn't before, if flushing comes with diarrhea, wheezing, or weight loss, or if hot flashes are disrupting your life. If you drink heavily most days and get sweats and shakes when you stop, talk to a doctor before quitting, because withdrawal can be dangerous.

**Does DHM stop hot flashes from alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that DHM stops hot flashes or the alcohol flush. Lab and animal research suggests it may help the body process alcohol, but human data is limited. It doesn't change menopause hot flashes or the genetic flush reaction, and drinking less remains the most reliable way to reduce alcohol-related heat and flushing.
